title: Review 5: Spots, open weaves, analysis, crimp and double cloth

quizzes.title: Key terms across the lectures
quizzes.intro: Terms from the last five design lectures.

questions.q: In a spot design, the “ground” is
options: The background weave around the spots
questions.explain: Small motifs are repeated on a plain or other simple ground weave.

questions.q: Huckaback is mainly used for
questions.explain: Its floats on a plain ground give a rough, absorbent surface.

questions.q: A mock leno
options: Crosses warp ends with a doup heald
Imitates the open look of leno on an ordinary dobby
questions.explain: Ends and picks are grouped so that they crowd together and leave gaps, without any crossing of ends.

questions.q: The first clue to the warp direction of a sample is
options: The selvedge, which runs parallel to the warp
questions.explain: When a selvedge is present there is no doubt; other clues are used when it is missing.

questions.q: Crimp percentage is
options: (Straightened yarn length − cloth length) ÷ cloth length
questions.explain: It measures how much longer the yarn is than the cloth it was taken from.

questions.q: A double cloth has
options: Two warps and two wefts forming a face layer and a back layer
questions.explain: Each layer weaves its own structure; stitching points can tie the layers together.

questions.q: The face of a fabric is usually the side with more lustre and the clearer weave.
questions.explain: Finish and print are also applied to the face.

questions.q: Which arrangement of spots spreads them most evenly, with no obvious lines?
questions.explain: The sateen order scatters the spots so that neither rows nor diagonals stand out.

questions.q: A stitching point in a double cloth is
options: A place where a thread of one layer interlaces with the other layer
A sewing stitch added after weaving
questions.explain: For example, a back end lifted over a face pick ties the two layers.

questions.q: A double cloth woven without any stitching can open out as a tube or a bag.
questions.explain: The layers are joined only at the edges, where the weft passes from one to the other.

quizzes.title: Linking the ideas
quizzes.intro: The reasoning behind distribution, analysis, crimp and layers.

questions.q: In a double cloth, when a back pick is inserted
options: All face ends must be lifted out of the way
All back ends must be lifted
questions.explain: The back pick must pass under the whole face layer, so every face end is up while the back ends weave their own pattern.

questions.q: When a spot is placed on a plain ground, the motif should start where it continues the plain order because otherwise
options: Long floats appear at its edges
questions.explain: A motif out of step with the ground breaks the plain interlacing next to it.

questions.q: Warp yarn in a sample usually feels stiffer than weft because
questions.explain: Size makes the warp harsher and harder to unravel.

questions.q: A weave with more crimp, for the same yarns and threads, gives a cloth that is
options: Thicker, more extensible and uses more yarn
questions.explain: The yarn follows a longer, wavier path.

questions.q: Why does a 2/2 twill have less crimp than plain weave in the jammed state?
options: Its threads interlace less often and float straight in between
questions.explain: About 13% against 21%: straight floats add length of cloth without adding bends.

questions.q: Huckaback absorbs water well because
options: Loose floats stand up from a firm plain ground
questions.explain: The floats give surface and softness; the plain blocks give strength.

questions.q: If one set of threads in a sample is two-fold and the other single, the folded yarn is almost always
questions.explain: Warp yarns must be stronger and more uniform, so folded yarns are normally used there.

questions.q: In a double cloth, a back end may be lifted on a face pick only as a deliberate stitch.
questions.explain: The rule keeps back ends down on face picks; breaking it at chosen points ties the layers.

questions.q: A sateen base of 5 with spot intervals of 6 ends and 8 picks gives a repeat of
questions.explain: Five positions × 6 ends = 30 ends, and five × 8 picks = 40 picks.

questions.q: In a dense warp-faced fabric the weft usually has more crimp than the warp.
questions.explain: In dense fabrics the set with more crimp is usually the warp; weft-faced cloths can be the reverse.

quizzes.title: Mixed calculations
quizzes.intro: Repeats, crimp and counts to work out.

questions.q: A yarn taken from 10.0 cm of cloth measures 10.9 cm when straightened. What is the crimp in percent?
A cloth 50 m long has 12% warp crimp. What length of each warp end does it contain, in metres?
A huckaback is drafted 1 2 1 2 1 3 4 3 4 3. How many heald frames does it need?
questions.explain: The draft uses healds 1 to 4.

questions.q: Spots are placed on a 5-end sateen base with intervals of 8 ends and 10 picks. How many ends are in the repeat?
questions.explain: 5 × 8 = 40 ends (and 5 × 10 = 50 picks).

questions.q: How many spots are there in one repeat of a design distributed on an 8-end sateen base?
questions.explain: One spot for each point of the base: 8.

questions.q: A sample has 30 ends per centimetre. How many ends per inch is that, to one decimal? (1 in = 2.54 cm)
questions.explain: 30 × 2.54 = 76.2 ends per inch.

questions.q: Forty threads, each 12.5 cm long when straightened, together weigh 0.15 g. What is the count in tex?
A double cloth has a 2/2 twill face and a plain back, with face and back ends alternating one and one. How many heald frames are needed in all?
questions.explain: 4 for the twill face and 2 for the plain back: 6 frames.

questions.q: A double cloth has 60 face ends per inch and 60 back ends per inch. How many ends per inch pass through the reed?
questions.explain: 60 + 60 = 120 ends per inch.

questions.q: In a jammed plain weave of equal yarns, yarn length per crossing is 2.094 d and spacing is 1.732 d. What is the crimp, in percent to one decimal?

quizzes.title: Case study
quizzes.intro: A sample on the analysis table: find its crimp, counts, sett and weight.

questions.q: What is the warp crimp in percent?
What is the weft crimp in percent?
What is the total length of the fifty warp threads in metres, to one decimal?
What is the warp count in tex?
What is the weft count in tex?
What is the warp count in Ne, to one decimal? Use Ne = 590.5 ÷ tex.
How many ends per inch does the cloth have, to the nearest whole number? (1 in = 2.54 cm)
questions.explain: 48 × 2.54 = 122 ends per inch.

questions.q: What weight of warp yarn is in one square metre of the cloth, in grams to one decimal?
What is the weight of the cloth in GSM, to the nearest whole number?
There is no selvedge on the sample. Which evidence best supports calling the 48-per-cm set the warp?
options: It is the finer yarn, more closely set and with more crimp
questions.explain: Warp is normally finer, stronger, set more densely and, in dense cloths, more crimped. All three point the same way here.

quizzes.case: A 10 cm × 10 cm sample of a plain cloth arrives for analysis. You count 48 ends and 32 picks per centimetre. Fifty warp threads pulled from the sample each measure 10.8 cm when straightened and together weigh 0.108 g. Fifty weft threads each measure 10.5 cm when straightened and together weigh 0.1575 g.

quizzes.title: Group challenge
quizzes.intro: Questions that need two of the lectures at once.

questions.q: A double cloth has a 3/1 twill face and a 2/2 twill back, ends alternating face and back. How many ends are in the full weave repeat?
questions.explain: Each layer repeats on 4 ends; alternating one and one doubles it: 8 ends.

questions.q: In that double cloth (3/1 twill face, 2/2 twill back), on a back pick, how many of the 4 face ends in the repeat are lifted?
questions.explain: Every face end is lifted on every back pick so that the back pick passes underneath.

questions.q: For the same double cloth, on a face pick, how many of the 8 ends in the repeat are lifted (no stitching)?
questions.explain: Only face ends lift, in the 3/1 order: 3 of the 4 face ends and none of the back ends = 3.

questions.q: A cloth is analysed at 100 ends per inch with 10% warp crimp, in a yarn of 20 tex. What weight of warp is in one square metre, in grams to one decimal? (1 m = 39.37 in)
Two samples have the same yarns and sett. Sample A is plain weave and B is a 2/2 twill. Which needs more warp length per metre of cloth?
options: A, because plain weave has more crimp
questions.explain: Plain weave bends the yarn at every crossing, so its crimp and yarn consumption are higher.

questions.q: A spot design on a plain ground shows long loose floats beside every motif. The most likely cause is
options: The motif was not started in step with the plain ground
questions.explain: This is the lecture’s “plain basis, alternate order” rule: the motif must continue the plain interlacing.

questions.q: A warp rib is found to have 57% warp crimp. How many metres of each warp end are needed for 100 m of cloth?
A mock leno can be woven on a dobby loom, while a true leno needs a doup heald to cross the ends.
questions.explain: That is why mock leno is the cheaper way to get an open, perforated look.

questions.q: During analysis, a sample shows a prominent twill line running along the direction that also has the higher thread count. That direction is most likely
options: Impossible to say from these clues
questions.explain: Design lines usually run warp-way and the sett is normally higher in the warp; both clues agree.

questions.q: A self-stitched double cloth has 8 picks in its repeat, alternating face and back. One stitch is made on each face pick. How many stitching points are there in the repeat?
questions.explain: Half of the 8 picks are face picks: 4 stitching points.
